summary: This proposed standard defines an optional IS-IS TLV called CAPABILITY, made up of sub-TLVs, with which a router can announce its capabilities within an IS-IS level or the whole routing domain. It obsoletes RFC 4971.

plainLanguage.summary: IS-IS routers often need to know what the other routers around them can do, so that they can plan paths together. This document gives them a general place to say so: one optional record that a router puts in its link state advertisements, carrying whatever pieces of information other specifications define.

subtitle: A way for IS-IS routers to tell each other what they can do.

tldr.problem: IS-IS routers often need to learn what other routers in their level, area or domain can do, for example for MPLS traffic engineering, but the protocol had no generic place to announce this.
tldr.mechanism: The Router CAPABILITY TLV, type 242, carries a Router ID, one octet of flags and optional sub-TLVs. The S flag decides whether it is flooded across the whole domain, and the D flag stops it looping between levels.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 4971 and fixes the IPv6-only case by allowing a Router ID of 0.0.0.0 when an IPv6 traffic engineering Router ID sub-TLV is present. The sub-TLVs themselves are defined elsewhere.

today: RFC 7981 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2016. It obsoletes RFC 4971 and has not been obsoleted or updated since, so it remains the standard way for an IS-IS router to advertise its capabilities.

sections.title: Why Routers Need to Announce Capabilities
sections.content:
There are several situations where it is useful for IS-IS routers to learn the capabilities of the other routers of their IS-IS level, area or routing domain. Three examples related to MPLS Traffic Engineering illustrate this. First, a mesh group: setting up a mesh of traffic engineering label switched paths requires significant configuration effort, and RFC 4972 proposes an auto-discovery mechanism in which every label switching router of a mesh advertises its mesh-group membership by means of IS-IS extensions. Second, point-to-multipoint traffic engineering label switched paths: a specific sub-TLV allows a label switching router to advertise its point-to-multipoint capabilities. Third, inter-area traffic engineering, which needs the advertisement of the IPv4 and or the IPv6 traffic engineering Router IDs.

The use of IS-IS for Path Computation Element discovery may also be considered and is discussed in the PCE working group.

The capabilities mentioned above require the specification of new sub-TLVs carried within the IS-IS Router CAPABILITY TLV defined in this document. The examples are given for the sake of illustration: the document proposes a generic capability advertising mechanism that is not limited to MPLS traffic engineering.

This document defines a new optional IS-IS TLV named CAPABILITY, formed of multiple sub-TLVs, which allows a router to announce its capabilities within an IS-IS level or the entire routing domain. Definition of the sub-TLVs themselves is outside the scope of this document, as is the specification of how an application may use the TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: Some jobs need the routers in a network to know what each other can do. Setting up a mesh of traffic engineering paths, for example, needs every router to say which group it belongs to. This document gives them a general place to say so, so that each kind of information can be defined separately.

sections.title: The IS-IS Router CAPABILITY TLV
sections.content:
The IS-IS Router CAPABILITY TLV is composed of one octet for the type, one octet that specifies the number of bytes in the value field, and a variable length value field that starts with 4 octets of Router ID, indicating the source of the TLV, followed by one octet of flags. A set of optional sub-TLVs may follow the flag field, formatted as described in RFC 5305. The type is 242, the length runs from 5 to 255, and the optional sub-TLVs occupy 0 to 250 octets.

Two bit flags are defined. The S bit, with value 0x01, decides the reach of the record: if it is set, the TLV MUST be flooded across the entire routing domain, and if it is not set, the TLV MUST NOT be leaked between levels. The bit MUST NOT be altered during the leaking. The D bit, with value 0x02, is set when the TLV is leaked from Level 2 to Level 1, and must be clear otherwise. TLVs with the D bit set MUST NOT be leaked from Level 1 to Level 2, which is what prevents the record from looping.

The TLV is OPTIONAL, and more than one IS-IS Router CAPABILITY TLV from the same source MAY be present.

IANA originally assigned the codepoint 242 to the IS-IS Router CAPABILITY TLV as described in RFC 4971, and has updated the entry in the TLV Codepoints Registry to refer to this document.
sections.plainLanguage: The record is small: a four octet identifier for the router that sent it, one octet of flags, and then whatever pieces of information other specifications define. Two of the flag bits matter: one says whether the record should travel across the whole routing domain, and the other records that it has already been copied down a level, so that it is not copied back up and forth forever.

sections.title: Elements of Procedure
sections.content:
The Router ID SHOULD be identical to the value advertised in the traffic engineering Router ID TLV of RFC 5305. If no traffic engineering Router ID is assigned, it SHOULD be identical to an IP interface address advertised by the originating IS-IS router. If the originating node does not support IPv4, the reserved value 0.0.0.0 MUST be used in the Router ID field and the IPv6 traffic engineering Router ID sub-TLV MUST be present. TLVs that have a Router ID of 0.0.0.0 and do not have the IPv6 traffic engineering Router ID sub-TLV present MUST NOT be used. These rules are the change this document makes to RFC 4971, which only allowed a 32-bit Router ID in the fixed header, a problem in an IPv6-only deployment where an IPv4 address may not be available.

When advertising capabilities with different flooding scopes, a router MUST originate a minimum of two IS-IS Router CAPABILITY TLVs, each carrying the set of sub-TLVs with the same flooding scope. So a router advertising two sets of capabilities, C1 with an area or level scope and C2 with a routing domain scope, originates one TLV with the S flag cleared carrying the sub-TLVs for C1, which will not be leaked into another level, and one TLV with the S flag set carrying the sub-TLVs for C2, which will be leaked into other IS-IS levels. When that second TLV is leaked from Level 2 to Level 1, the D bit is set in the Level 1 LSP advertisement.

To prevent the use of stale TLVs, a system MUST NOT use an IS-IS Router CAPABILITY TLV present in an LSP of a system that is not currently reachable via Level x paths, where x is the level in which the sending system advertised the TLV. This applies whether or not the sending system is the originator of the TLV. When the TLV is not used, whether because of a lack of reachability or an unusable Router ID, leaking it is one of the uses prohibited under these conditions. The example in the document: if a Level 1 router A generates the TLV and floods it to two routers, S and T, they will flood it into the Level 2 domain. If the Level 1 area then partitions so that A and S are in one partition and T in another, IP routing will still work, but if A issues a revised TLV or stops advertising it, S will follow suit while T keeps advertising the old version until the LSP times out. Routers in other areas have to choose between T's copy and S's copy of A's TLV and have no reliable way to choose, so making sure that T stops leaking A's information removes the possibility that other routers use stale information.

In IS-IS, the atomic unit of the update process is a TLV, or, for TLVs that allow multiple entries in the value field, an entry in that field. If an update to an entry is advertised in a different LSP fragment from the advertisement it replaces, other systems can temporarily hold either zero copies or two copies of an advertisement, depending on the order in which the fragments arrive. Wherever possible, an implementation SHOULD advertise the update in the same LSP fragment as the advertisement it replaces, and where that is not possible the two affected fragments should be flooded as an atomic action. A receiving system can minimize disruption by employing a holddown time before processing the update, so that several fragments of the same update can arrive first. Where a receiving system has two copies from the same system with conflicting information for a given sub-TLV, the procedure for choosing which copy to use is undefined.
sections.plainLanguage: Two rules matter in practice. A router that has both a local and a domain-wide set of capabilities sends two records, one for each scope, because a record cannot be both. And a router must stop using a capability record from a neighbour it can no longer reach, so that a partitioned area does not leave stale information circulating in the rest of the domain.

sections.title: Routers That Do Not Support the TLV
sections.content:
Routers that do not support the IS-IS Router CAPABILITY TLV MUST silently ignore the TLVs and continue processing the other TLVs in the same LSP. Routers that do not support specific sub-TLVs carried within it MUST silently ignore the unsupported sub-TLVs and continue processing those that are supported. How partial support affects the operation of the capabilities advertised is outside the scope of this document.

For the Router CAPABILITY TLVs with domain-wide scope, originated by Level 1 routers, to be flooded across the entire domain, at least one Level 1 to Level 2 router in every area of the domain MUST support the TLV.

If leaking of the TLV is required, the entire CAPABILITY TLV MUST be leaked into another level without change, except for the changes to the flags described earlier, even if it contains sub-TLVs that the router doing the leaking does not support.
sections.plainLanguage: A router that has never heard of this record simply skips it and carries on with the rest of the link state advertisement. That is what makes it safe to deploy: older routers ignore what they do not understand, and a router that copies the record into another level copies all of it, even the parts it cannot read.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Any new security issues raised by the procedures in this document depend on the opportunity for link state advertisements to be snooped and modified, whose ease or difficulty has not been altered. As the LSPs may now contain additional information regarding router capabilities, that new information would also become available to an attacker. Specifications based on this mechanism need to describe the security considerations around the disclosure and modification of their information.

An integrity mechanism, such as the ones defined in RFC 5304 or RFC 5310, should be applied if there is high risk resulting from modification of capability information.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything the protocol sends is visible to anyone who can watch the routing protocol, and that includes the new capability information. Where it would matter, for instance if the information guided traffic that an attacker could redirect, the existing IS-IS authentication mechanisms should be used to protect it.

sections.title: The Codepoint and the Changes from RFC 4971
sections.content:
IANA originally assigned a TLV codepoint for the IS-IS Router CAPABILITY TLV, 242, as described in RFC 4971, and has updated that entry in the TLV Codepoints Registry to refer to this document.

RFC 4971 only allowed a 32-bit Router ID in the fixed header of TLV 242. That is problematic in an IPv6-only deployment, where an IPv4 address may not be available. This document therefore specifies that the Router ID SHOULD be identical to the value advertised in the Traffic Engineering Router ID TLV, 134, if one is available; that if no traffic engineering Router ID is assigned, the Router ID SHOULD be identical to an IP interface address advertised by the originating IS-IS router; and that if the originating node does not support IPv4, the reserved value 0.0.0.0 MUST be used in the Router ID field and the IPv6 TE Router ID sub-TLV MUST be present in the TLV. In addition, some clarifying editorial changes have been made.
sections.plainLanguage: The only real change from the earlier version is how the router's own identifier is filled in, so that a network that has no IPv4 addresses at all can still use the record. The rest is wording.

viz.caption: THE CODED POINTS IN THE CAPABILITY TLV

items.label: TLV type
items.desc: The codepoint for the IS-IS Router CAPABILITY TLV, assigned in RFC 4971 and now referring to RFC 7981.

items.label: S bit
items.desc: If set, the TLV MUST be flooded across the entire routing domain. If not set, it MUST NOT be leaked between levels, and the bit MUST NOT be altered during leaking.

items.label: D bit
items.desc: Set when the TLV is leaked from Level 2 to Level 1, and clear otherwise. A TLV with the D bit set MUST NOT be leaked from Level 1 to Level 2, to prevent looping.

viz.caption: TWO TLVs FOR TWO FLOODING SCOPES

viz.caption: WHAT A ROUTER THAT DOES NOT SUPPORT THE TLV MUST DO

items.title: Unsupported TLV
items.text: Silently ignore it and continue processing the other TLVs in the same LSP.

items.title: Unsupported sub-TLV
items.text: Silently ignore the unsupported sub-TLVs and carry on with the ones that are supported.

items.title: Leaking
items.text: The entire CAPABILITY TLV must be leaked into another level without change, even if it holds sub-TLVs the leaking router does not support.

items.title: Domain-wide flooding
items.text: At least one L1/L2 router in every area of the domain must support the TLV.
